To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the forecasts are rational; (2) the forecast errors are unbiased; (3) the forecasts are not excessively smooth; (4) the forecasters do not systematically under- or over-react to news; and (5) the forecasts do not systematically over- or under-estimate the volatility of the economy.

(i) judgmental adjustments tend to reduce the variation in the forecasts over time, (ii) judgmental adjustments do not tend to reduce the forecast errors, (iii) judgmental adjustments have a small effect on the rationality properties of the forecasts, and (iv) judgmental adjustments appear to have little effect on the underlying output-inﬂation trade-oﬀ implicit in the model.

a) the rationality of published forecasts is not significantly affected by the inclusion of judgmental adjustments; b) the revisions to published forecasts are significantly correlated with the revisions to the underlying model-based forecasts and the revisions to the judgmental adjustments; and c) the inclusion of judgment adjustments reduces the variation in forecasts over time, and alters the underlying output-infla-tion trade-off implicit in model-based forecasts.

the question of whether or not published forecasts are biased in the sense that they do not reflect all of the information that is available to the forecaster at the time the forecast is made.
the role of judgemental adjustments in macroeconomic forecasting.
the question: How does the use of judgemental adjustments affect the rationality and accuracy of forecasts?

the evidence on the rationality and the effects of judgemental adjustments is not conclusive, and is in fact contradictory, and the debate on these issues is far from over.

the rational expectations assumption is a very powerful tool in macroeconomic analysis.
